video_title: Building Cyber Defense for the Agentic Era
gist: Kevin, Mandiant's founder and now at Armadin, argues that AI-driven offense will make legacy pentesting and human-in-the-loop detect/respond obsolete. Armadin's agent swarms have found 90+ zero days, black-box, at Fortune 500 customers since January 2026, and its next product pushes compensating controls into the EDR and firewall platforms (CrowdStrike, Palo Alto, Fortinet). He says open-weight models already match closed ones on full cyber kill chains (8 of 20 for every model, with closed models only faster), so attacks are bottlenecked by anonymous GPU access, not by model capability. He calls the next year a near-term offense-advantaged window and says every security tech stack will be replaced within two years.

insights.claim: AI-driven cyberattacks are only in the 'first inning'. The guest says criminal adoption is held back mainly by the cost and availability of models and GPUs, not by capability, and that open models are already good enough.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Slowing down frontier models will not contain cyber risk, so demand for AI defense does not depend on frontier-lab policy.
insights.quote: the whole let's slow down the models. We don't want cyber risk too late. the open models are already good enough

insights.claim: The guest predicts that once GPUs can be used anonymously, criminal AI-driven attacks will rise sharply, because attribution risk is what currently deters criminals.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Anonymous GPU or compute markets are a leading indicator for a jump in criminal attack volume and in security spending.
insights.quote: the minute you have anonymous availability of GPUs, you'll see far more criminal attacks

insights.claim: AI attacks seen in the wild today are crude compared with what Armadin has built internally (about 25,000 coordinated agents). They are recognizable because AI does things like re-breaking into a host it already compromised after moving laterally.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: There is a short window before attacker AI catches up with state-of-the-art offensive agent systems, so defenders have limited time.
insights.quote: there's 25,000 agents all in concert, all working together doing really, really smart things without going on bizarre fishing trips

insights.claim: AI's advantage over human attackers is scale and speed. Humans had to pick a single path into a network, while AI exhausts every route at once, and AI does in a microsecond what 70 humans could not do.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: The attack surface that matters is now every path, not the likeliest one, which favors continuous and comprehensive testing tools over point-in-time ones.
insights.quote: What AI does in a microscond would take 70 humans they can't even do it. It's apples to oranges.

insights.claim: Offensive security does not need the most advanced model. Finding exploitable vulnerabilities works on code, a structured language and process, which is the kind of task AI excels at.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Cyber offense capability spreads quickly to cheap and open models, so frontier-model gating does not create a moat for attackers or defenders.
insights.quote: That is code. That's a structured language, a structured process. Because it's structured, AI is going to be great at it.

insights.claim: Armadin built 20 full real-world kill chains as an eval. No model, open-weight or the most advanced closed model, completed more than 8. All models plateaued at the same place, with closed models only reaching it faster and differing on cost.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: The closed-versus-open gap in cyber is compressed to speed and cost, so a premium frontier model is not a durable edge for cyber-offense products, and open-weight risk is real.
insights.quote: We tested the open weight ones and the most advanced closed models. They all found eight.

insights.claim: AI lowers the skill floor for attackers. Less capable, less technical actors will look far more successful, and attribution (nation, criminal, or individual) will become harder.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Expect more attack volume from more actors and weaker deterrence through attribution, which expands the market beyond the high-end targets nation-states hit.
insights.quote: less capable attackers, >> less technical, less successful are going to appear way more successful. It's the equalizer

insights.claim: Untuned AI offense is not stealthy. Without heavy post-training and a human in the loop, a prompted attack is loud and sloppy but more comprehensive, and so probably more effective.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: In the near term AI attacks may be detectable but overwhelming, so the defensive bottleneck is response speed, not visibility.
insights.quote: right now AI is not a surreptitious action on offense

insights.claim: Nation-state cyber espionage has historically used a 'sniper round' approach, going deep on narrow target sets such as 30 defense contractors. The guest says AI pushes toward a 'drone swarm' doctrine of burning tokens on a target, and nations are now rethinking when to swarm and when to snipe.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Breadth of nation-state targeting could widen beyond defense and government into the broader enterprise base.
insights.quote: with AI I think becomes more like a drone swarm

insights.claim: There is a near-term 'desperation moment' on both sides. Offensive operators in Iran or Russia want to get in and pre-position now, while defenders rush to patch every window, because AI temporarily advantages offense.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Expect elevated breach activity and urgent, budget-insensitive security spending over the next year.
insights.quote: if you're on offense in Iran or Russia, you have a desperation in a moment of get in now

insights.claim: The guest frames AI as a near-term pain that advantages offense but a long-term gain: autonomous AI defense trained by AI offense will ultimately do a far better job than humans watching packets.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: The investment thesis is a long-duration build-out of AI-native defense after a period of elevated incidents.
insights.quote: we have near-term pain in the AI age that it advantages offense, period

themes.theme: Armadin product: continuous AI red teaming

insights.claim: Armadin's 'hyper attack' throws a swarm of agents at a customer to map every service, route, system and asset, sometimes producing terabytes of metadata. That builds an attacker's-view 'metadata twin', which Armadin then polls cheaply like a heartbeat so it can attack only what changes.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Continuous, change-triggered testing turns pentesting into a recurring, always-on subscription spend.
insights.quote: we throw a drone swarm of agents at you and we map your network

insights.claim: Constant model-driven attack pressure is cost-prohibitive and unnecessary. The guest says re-testing should be triggered by three things: the threat changes (new models or intelligence), the network changes, or an ad hoc audit such as before a board meeting.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Usage, and the vendor's token cost, scale with network churn and with model releases. Large, fast-changing networks are the highest-value customers.

insights.claim: Since January 2026, Armadin says it has found more than 90 zero days at Fortune 500 customer sites in production, black-box from the internet, without source code or credentials. It typically calls the CISO within 48 hours reporting remote code execution in the DMZ, and the customer goes into incident mode.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This is hard evidence that AI-assisted offense finds exploitable zero days in major enterprises, supporting rapid adoption of AI red teaming.
insights.quote: Armadin since January of this year n in 2026, we have found over 90 zero days at customer sites all in production

insights.claim: The guest dismisses source-code scanning à la Mythos, which finds thousands of vulnerabilities, as noise. He says the value is in verified, exploitable, outside-in findings with zero false positives.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Differentiation in AI AppSec will come from exploit verification rather than raw vulnerability counts, which bears on how to judge vendor claims.
insights.quote: you can scan source code and find vulnerabilities and you find thousands of them. That's noise.

insights.claim: Humans found most of Armadin's 90+ zero days, with AI doing 90%+ of the tedious work. The guest says the most recent few zero days were found by the technology itself, which he calls 'making the turn'.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This is an inflection signal that autonomous zero-day discovery is now real, which compresses the time from bug to exploit for attackers too.
insights.quote: the last few zero days tech found it

insights.claim: Armadin post-trains its models with real red teamers and exploit developers, and red teamers write most of its evals. The guest argues that securing and evaluating agents requires domain expertise that pure AI researchers lack.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Domain-expert data and evals are the moat for vertical AI security companies, more than model access.
insights.quote: our evals most of the time are made by the red teamers

insights.claim: Armadin's team has red-teamed 99 of the Fortune 100 over their careers. Operators typically have about 15 years of offensive experience.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Existing enterprise relationships give Armadin distribution, which is relevant given the go-to-market race it describes.
insights.quote: I think we've red teamed literally 99 of the Fortune 100 throughout our careers

themes.theme: Category disruption: pentesting, autonomous defense, SOC

insights.claim: The guest says legacy pentesting and vulnerability scanning (Tenable, Rapid7, Qualys) is a hygiene step that lists known CVEs without proving exploitability. He says AI red teaming will replace pentesting over time, because continuous red teaming was always desirable but too costly in money and people until agents arrived.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This is a disruption risk to incumbent vulnerability-management vendors. Watch for share loss or M&A as AI red teaming moves into budgets.
insights.quote: I think it'll replace pen testing over time

insights.claim: The guest predicts AI offensive testing will become as ubiquitous as antivirus, mirroring how CrowdStrike redefined AV into EDR, a far bigger category.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This frames AI red teaming as a new mandatory budget line, a potential new large security category.
insights.quote: we will be as ubiquitous as AV

insights.claim: Armadin's second product, 'Armadin Blue', turns findings about exploitable risk into autonomous compensating controls pushed through existing defense platforms. It is being built with CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks (Pan) and is meant to inform others such as Fortinet.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Incumbent EDR and firewall platforms become actuation layers for AI-driven defense, which reinforces their position and creates partnership value for AI red-team vendors.
insights.quote: we're working with Crowdstrike on it and they know it has to exist. We're working with Pan on it.

insights.claim: The guest predicts CISOs will get autonomous defense 'even if you don't ask for it', through platforms they have already bought. Compensating controls will be rudimentary in the next few months but standard within a year.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Platform vendors that ship autonomous response will capture value. Watch EDR and firewall roadmaps over the next 12 months.
insights.quote: you're going to see autonomous defense happen even if you don't ask for it

insights.claim: The guest argues that a bad automated patch that blocks an attacker is better than an intrusion, and that the cyber domain is moving too fast to keep humans in tactical defense decisions.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Enterprise tolerance for automated, possibly disruptive controls is rising, which lifts adoption barriers for autonomous security.
insights.quote: I I'd rather have a bad patch stopping a bad guy from getting in >> than have an intrusion

insights.claim: The guest says humans in the detect-and-respond loop will be too slow. Prevention will be governed by AI, detection and response will be done by AI, and whole SOC processes will disappear.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This is a headwind for labor-heavy MDR and SOC services models and a tailwind for autonomous detection and response vendors.
insights.quote: if you have humans in the detect and respond loop, you're going to be too slow

insights.claim: When Armadin's agentic internal command-and-control gets inside a network, it spreads 'at a speed that is shocking', doing a thousand things at once. The guest likens a breached defense to a balloon popping, so internal traps must fire without humans.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Defense in depth with automated internal tripwires and containment becomes mandatory, a demand driver for deception and automated containment tools.
insights.quote: it proliferates at a speed that is shocking

insights.claim: CISOs are re-examining headcount, workforce and processes for the AI era, but the guest says it is too soon to tell where SOC structures and defense architectures land.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Budgets are in flux, so vendor wins in the next year may be volatile and land-grab driven.

insights.claim: The guest says he knows of no large enterprise that is not actively scanning for exposure in real time. CIOs, CISOs, product teams and business lines are war-rooming together, and one sophisticated company reallocated a large share of its engineers and researchers to fortifying its own systems.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder) and David (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Security has become a cross-functional, all-hands priority, which supports near-term security budget growth even beyond IT.
insights.quote: there's no way to make the next year pretty

insights.claim: The guest says every cybersecurity tech stack will be different within two years, with incumbents ripped out and replaced, a 'tailwind of a lifetime' in cyber.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder) and David (a16z host)
insights.so_what: Expect high churn and replacement cycles in security. Favor AI-native entrants and watch incumbents for displacement.
insights.quote: in cyber security, every single tech stack is going to be different over the next two years

themes.theme: Mythos moment and AI lab safety

insights.claim: The guest says the 'Mythos moment' was the marketing catalyst that convinced everyone the threat had changed, prompting vendors to scan their own software, though experts had seen AI offense coming long before.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Frontier-model capability releases act as demand shocks for security spending, so watch future model launches as catalysts.
insights.quote: the mythos moment from a marketing standpoint got everybody to go okay threats changed

insights.claim: Discussing the Hugging Face incident, the guest says that in every technology shift the industry underestimates adversaries, and here it underestimated the models. The labs could have stopped it with deterministic guardrails but were in a lunar-landing-style race.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: AI lab safety failures are likely to recur, which creates demand for agent security and guardrail tooling that combines AI with security expertise.
insights.quote: It's been my experience in every technical modality shift, we underestimate the adversar's capability

insights.claim: Armadin cages its offensive agents with a hypervisor, host-based lockdown, a proxy, passive inspection of every prompt, deterministic rules, and classifiers on all inbound and outbound traffic that escalate to humans. Most agent kills happen because the agent is wasting money, not because of safety.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This is a template for agent-safety architecture, and it suggests that inference cost management is a core operating lever for agentic security firms.
insights.quote: the majority of the time if we kill an agent, it's probably nothing to do with safety. It's that the agent's wasting money

insights.claim: The guest argues that over-deterministic guardrails sacrifice the creativity of frontier models. The art of running offensive AI safely is to let it out some, find the line, and use trained classifiers, which means no one can be 100% certain of outcomes.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: There is a trade-off between agent safety and capability, so tooling that resolves it (classifiers, human escalation) has value.
insights.quote: if you get too deterministic and disallowed too much, you're probably not leveraging the creativity of it

insights.claim: Like the earlier shift to the cloud, the industry must learn what an 'AI breach' looks like. The guest says model companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI will need better logging, audit trails and forensics so incidents do not take two weeks to reconstruct.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This points to an emerging category in AI forensics and agent audit logging, plus potential compliance requirements on model providers.
insights.quote: We now have to learn what's an AI breach look like

insights.claim: The guest calls Armadin the 'third wave of intel'. Antivirus signatures were the first, Mandiant-style learning from breach response was the second (the layer CrowdStrike now owns), and finding your own problems before any victim is compromised is the third.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This positions proactive AI offense as the next platform layer after EDR, with a potentially similar scale of opportunity.
insights.quote: I actually look at Armen as just the third wave of intel

insights.claim: The guest contrasts Mandiant, founded in February 2004, self-funded and profitable with no competition because nobody believed 'breaches are inevitable', with Armadin, which needs heavy funding to build sales, go-to-market and international reach fast in a crowded market.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Armadin is likely to raise capital and scale go-to-market aggressively. Expect funding rounds and competition in AI red teaming.
insights.quote: I feel like we have an 80 mph tailwind, but we don't have a sales force

insights.claim: The guest cites Wiz reaching over $100M ARR within 18 months of its first release as the benchmark Armadin aims to beat. He believes consumer-AI revenue ramps cannot be replicated in enterprise security sales.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This sets an explicit growth target, Wiz-like or faster, for evaluating Armadin and similar AI security startups.
insights.quote: Whiz got to over 100 million in AR in 18 months from their first release, right? We're going to try to beat that.

insights.claim: The guest says IP is short-lived ('whatever we're doing today, someone else is doing in six months'), so the real differentiators are go-to-market, brand and delighted marquee customers such as money-center banks, top retailers and airlines.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: In AI security, judge startups on marquee customer traction and distribution more than technology claims.
insights.quote: whatever we're doing today, someone else is doing in six months

insights.claim: Because the product changes every two weeks, the guest argues enterprise security sales still need people-heavy go-to-market and weekly sales training. AI does not reduce sales headcount here and may increase reliance on it, because customers cannot track the changes themselves.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: Do not assume AI compresses sales and marketing costs for enterprise security vendors, at least for now.
insights.quote: people still buy from people

insights.claim: The guest cites a text claiming 43% of RSA main-stage keynotes about a year ago were Mandiant alumni, a statistic he says he never verified.
insights.speaker: Kevin (Armadin co-founder, Mandiant founder)
insights.so_what: This illustrates the depth of the Mandiant talent network that Armadin can recruit from and sell into.
insights.quote: 43% of the RSA mainstage keynotes are Mandian alumni
